fields.Back: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — one or more containers that share the same network namespace (IP, port space) and storage volumes, and are always scheduled together on the same node.

fields.Front: What's the relationship between a Deployment and a ReplicaSet?
fields.Back: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets: it creates a new ReplicaSet whenever the Pod template changes and orchestrates the rollout, scaling, and rollback. You typically create/manage Deployments, not ReplicaSets, directly.

fields.Front: What does a Kubernetes Service of type NodePort do?
fields.Back: Exposes the Service on a static port (30000-32767 by default) on every node's IP, so external traffic can reach it via <NodeIP>:<NodePort>, in addition to still getting a normal ClusterIP.

fields.Front: What does a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer do?
fields.Back: Provisions an external load balancer via the cloud provider (e.g. an AWS ELB) that routes external traffic into the Service, which then load-balances across the matching Pods. Builds on top of NodePort/ClusterIP.

fields.Front: What's the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret in Kubernetes?
fields.Back: Both inject configuration into Pods (as env vars or mounted files), but a Secret is meant for sensitive data — stored base64-encoded (not encrypted by default) with tighter access controls — while a ConfigMap holds non-sensitive plain configuration.

fields.Front: What is a Kubernetes Namespace used for?
fields.Back: A virtual partition of a single physical cluster used to isolate and organize groups of resources (e.g. per team or environment), scoping resource names and enabling per-namespace quotas and RBAC.

fields.Front: What does the kubelet do on each node?
fields.Back: An agent running on every node that makes sure the containers described in Pod specs assigned to that node are running and healthy, and reports node/Pod status back to the control plane.

fields.Front: What does the Kubernetes scheduler do?
fields.Back: Watches for newly created Pods that have no assigned node, and picks a suitable node for each based on resource requirements, affinity/anti-affinity rules, and taints/tolerations.

fields.Front: How do you list all Pods with kubectl?
fields.Back: kubectl get pods for the current namespace; add -A / --all-namespaces for every namespace, or -n <namespace> for a specific one.

fields.Front: How do you view logs for one container inside a multi-container Pod?
fields.Back: kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name> — the -c flag is only required when the Pod has more than one container.

What's the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
fields.Back: A liveness probe checks whether a container is still healthy; on failure, Kubernetes restarts the container. A readiness probe checks whether a container is ready to serve traffic; on failure, the Pod is pulled from Service endpoints but NOT restarted.

fields.Front: During a Deployment rolling update, how does Kubernetes avoid downtime by default?
fields.Back: It incrementally replaces old Pods with new ones: it creates new Pods and waits for them to pass their readiness probe before terminating old ones, bounded by the maxSurge and maxUnavailable settings of the rolling update strategy.
Automatically scales the number of Pod replicas in a Deployment or ReplicaSet up or down based on observed metrics (commonly CPU or memory utilization) to track a target value.

An API object that manages external HTTP/HTTPS access into cluster Services, providing host/path-based routing rules, TLS termination, and a single external entry point — it requires an Ingress controller to actually implement the routing.

fields.Front: Write a minimal Kubernetes Deployment YAML for an nginx app with 3 replicas.
fields.Back:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80

fields.Front: How does a Kubernetes Service know which Pods to route traffic to?
fields.Back: Via label selectors — the Service's selector field is matched against Pod labels, and any Pod with matching labels becomes an endpoint the Service load-balances across; membership is tracked continuously, not as a static list.
A Kubernetes controller that ensures a specified number of identical Pod replicas are running at all times, creating or deleting Pods as needed to match the desired count.

fields.Text: A Kubernetes Service of type {{c1::ClusterIP}} (the default) exposes a stable virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster.
The Kubernetes control plane consists of the {{c1::API server}}, {{c2::etcd}} (the cluster state store), the {{c3::scheduler}}, and the {{c4::controller manager}}.
fields.Extra: Typically runs on dedicated control-plane/master nodes.

fields.Text: kubectl {{c1::apply}} -f deployment.yaml declaratively creates or updates resources to match the YAML file, while kubectl {{c2::delete}} -f deployment.yaml removes the resources it defines.
